table.md:
| الرمز | المدينة | עיר | السكان | ملاحظات |
|---|---|---|--:|---|
| RUH | الرياض | ריאד | 7,676,654 | عاصمة المملكة العربية السعودية وأكبر مدنها من حيث عدد السكان. |
| JED | جدة | ג'דה | 3,751,722 | ميناء رئيسي على البحر الأحمر |
| TLV | تل أبيب | תל אביב | 474,530 | מרכז כלכלי ותרבותי, ידועה בחופים ובחיי הלילה שלה. |

understanding.purpose: Compare cities identified by code, with Arabic and Hebrew names, population figures, and descriptive notes.
understanding.reading: Read each row from right to left, matching the code and two city names before comparing populations and consulting the notes. Wrapped notes will largely determine row height.
groups: Columns 2 and 3 give the same kind of information: city names in Arabic and Hebrew.
Columns 1 and 4 contain compact codes and population figures that support quick scanning.
Column 5 contains descriptive notes and can use the vertical space created by wrapping.
keep_intact: Individual words in city names and notes

preferred.name: r0A
preferred.note: Give notes the most room while preserving Arabic names and figures, accepting wraps in multiword Hebrew names.

preferred.name: r2A
preferred.note: Reduce the Hebrew column to its 52px minimum for intact words and give the recovered space to notes. This preserves the existing wrap in the multiword Hebrew name while giving notes their greatest available width without splitting individual words.

acceptable.name: r1A
acceptable.note: Give Hebrew 3px more room while retaining the minimum widths needed to keep the Arabic names, codes, and population figures intact. Test whether the small increase improves Hebrew wrapping without materially lengthening notes.

acceptable.name: r1B
acceptable.note: Test a larger shift from notes to Hebrew as a middle ground between r0A and r0B. The notes retain 72px of text space, while Hebrew gains 6px over r0A.

bad.name: r0B
bad.note: Favor both city-name columns for easy cross-language comparison, with notes wrapping more often.
bad.why: The extra width given to the Hebrew city column does not keep the longest city name on one line, while the narrower notes column creates many short lines and much taller rows.

bad.name: r0C
bad.note: Share room between Hebrew names and notes by allowing longer Arabic city names to wrap.
bad.why: The Arabic city column is too narrow: its header wraps and الرياض splits within the word.

bad.name: r2B
bad.note: Give Hebrew enough room for its longest name on one line. The notes column falls 2px below the stated minimum for its longest word, so this tests whether the cleaner city-name comparison is worth a possible mid-word split in the notes.
bad.why: Keeping the Hebrew city names on one line takes so much space from notes that the notes header wraps and the prose breaks into very short lines, making the table much taller.

rationale: r0A and r2A have identical widths and rendering. They keep headers, identifiers, population figures and individual words intact while giving the prose notes the largest share of the available width. The Hebrew name תל אביב wraps at a word boundary, a reasonable exchange for more readable notes and shorter rows.

general: Allocate width according to content and reading role; prose often benefits more from extra width than short identifiers.
Keep identifiers, numbers and individual words intact, and judge wrapping by its effect on whole rows.
specific: The two city columns serve parallel roles, but their different scripts and contents do not require equal widths.
In this viewport, keeping the longest Hebrew city name on one line substantially constrains the notes column.

tradeoffs: A designer might favor r1A or r1B for a little more room around Hebrew city names, accepting the extra wrapping in notes and a taller final row. r2B keeps both city names on one line but pays a much larger price in notes readability.
uncertain: The ranges report only the tested preferred widths; nearby pixel values were not rendered, so equally good intervals cannot be established from these candidates.

critique.good: All headers, codes, population figures, and individual words remain intact. The Arabic names have enough room, and the notes receive the most space of the three designs, keeping the rows comparatively compact.
critique.problems: The narrow notes column produces tall rows and leaves substantial empty space under the shorter entries. The Hebrew name תל אביב wraps, although it remains readable as two intact words.
critique.cause: The notes have 78px of text space at a width of 99px; the Hebrew column has 31px of text space at 52px.

critique.good: The wider Hebrew column gives its names more room, while the headers, codes, figures, and individual words remain intact.
critique.problems: The notes become a narrow stack of short lines, making the first and last rows much taller and weakening the sense of each row as a unit. The wider Hebrew column does not prevent תל אביב from wrapping in the render.
critique.cause: Moving 20px from notes to Hebrew leaves notes only 58px of text space at 79px, while the 72px Hebrew column is still 2px short of its stated one-line content width including padding.

critique.good: The notes retain nearly as much width as in r0A, and the Hebrew column has more room.
critique.problems: The Arabic header wraps and الرياض splits within the word, damaging both the header hierarchy and the readability of a city name. The taller header and last row also make the table longer than r0A.
critique.cause: The 55px Arabic column leaves only 34px of text space, less than the 45px needed for its longest unbreakable word.

critique.good: Codes, Arabic city names, population figures and headers remain intact. The right-to-left sequence is easy to follow, and each row stays visually distinct.
critique.problems: The notes form a narrow, dense block with substantial empty space in the other cells of the taller rows. The Hebrew name תל אביב wraps, though its words remain intact.
critique.cause: The 96px notes column leaves 75px for text, forcing extensive wrapping. The 55px Hebrew column leaves 34px, less than the 53px needed for its longest one-line name.

critique.good: The compact fields and headers remain intact, and the rows preserve the same clear reading order as r1A.
critique.problems: The notes are still dense and tall, while the extra width given to the Hebrew column produces no visible improvement over r1A: תל אביב still wraps.
critique.cause: The 58px Hebrew column leaves only 37px for text, still short of the 53px needed to keep the name on one line. Moving those 3px from notes leaves that column at 93px without changing the overall row heights.

critique.good: The headers remain on one line, and codes, population figures, and individual words stay intact. The wider notes column keeps the rows substantially shorter than in r2B.
critique.problems: The notes are still a narrow, dense stack, making rows tall and leaving large areas of white space in the other columns. The Hebrew name for Tel Aviv wraps onto two lines.
critique.cause: The 99px notes column leaves 78px for text. The 52px Hebrew column leaves 31px, enough for each word but not the full 53px name.

critique.good: The 74px Hebrew column keeps multiword city names on one line, making that column easier to scan. Codes and population figures remain intact.
critique.problems: The notes header splits, and the notes form very tall, narrow blocks. The extra height produces large empty areas in the other columns and weakens the sense of each row as a unit.
critique.cause: Increasing the Hebrew column from 52px to 74px reduces the notes column from 99px to 77px. Its 56px text area is narrower than the 58px header and leaves little room for note text.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r0B.why: The narrow notes column produces many short lines and very tall rows, while the other columns have substantial unused space.

r1A.why: Numbers and Arabic city names stay intact, and the notes are more readable than in A. The Hebrew name for Tel Aviv wraps.

r0A.why: The notes have the most comfortable line lengths, while population figures and Arabic city names stay intact. The Hebrew name for Tel Aviv wraps.

ref_equal.why: Population figures break across lines, the notes header splits, and the narrow notes column makes the rows very tall.

r1B.why: Population figures and Arabic city names stay intact, and the notes remain readable. The Hebrew name for Tel Aviv wraps.

ref_auto.why: The notes have reasonable line lengths and the numbers stay intact, but both Arabic and Hebrew versions of Tel Aviv wrap.

raw.unsure: B, C and E are close; their small width differences make the balance between notes and city names difficult to judge at this image size.

ref_equal.why: Population figures split across lines, the notes header breaks, and the very narrow notes column produces a long, fragmented table.

r0B.why: Population figures and headers stay intact, but the narrow notes column makes the rows tall and difficult to scan.

r1A.why: The wider notes column improves the reading rhythm while keeping population figures intact. The Hebrew name תל אביב still wraps.

r1B.why: Population figures remain intact and the notes have more room than in B, though the Hebrew name תל אביב wraps and the notes remain dense.

ref_auto.why: Notes and numbers read reasonably well, but both the Arabic and Hebrew names for Tel Aviv wrap, weakening comparison across the city columns.

r0A.why: Population figures and Arabic city names stay intact, and the notes have a useful share of the width. The Hebrew name תל אביב wraps.

raw.unsure: C, D and F are close; their small width differences and resulting line breaks are difficult to judge precisely at this image scale.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
